Let’s take a moment to explore Chapter 7: Communication Without Words.
Most of us don’t even think about how much we rely on language. Words just... flow, right? They shape what we think, how we feel, and they help us connect with others.
But for animals—and for many folks on the autism spectrum—communication is often something different. It’s not about words at all. It’s a dance of gestures, sounds, and those moments when you simply share attention.
Imagine this: a teenager sitting on the porch with their dog, just tossing a ball back and forth. There’s no talking, but everything that matters is being said. The dog’s tail wags, the teen grins, and in that instant, they’re completely in sync.
It’s such a simple scene, but it shows something deeply true—relationships are built on so much more than words.
Animals are masters of this wordless language. Horses? They flatten their ears when they’re annoyed. Dogs do that playful bow to invite you in. And birds—well, they sing not just for the joy of it, but to mark their territory or attract a mate.
These signals might seem subtle, but they’re loaded with meaning. And to truly get them, you have to do more than just listen to words—you have to notice how something is said, or shown.
Now, for people with autism, this kind of nonverbal communication can be both tricky and powerful. Some find it tough to read a face or catch the tone of someone’s voice. Others, though, are incredibly tuned in to these little cues. Routines, rituals, and shared activities can become a way to connect—one that doesn’t depend on conversation.
The story shifts back to the woman in the cattle yard. She’s learned to “speak” the animals’ language by moving slowly, skipping sudden gestures, and guiding them with her body, not force. Over time, you can see a change—the animals get calmer, more willing to follow her lead.
It’s a real lesson in patience and humility, isn’t it? Communication takes effort, and it’s a two-way street. You have to be willing to meet others right where they are.
There’s also something beautiful about the power of silence. Sometimes, the best way to connect is to simply be there—to listen without jumping in, without expecting anything. In our noisy world, that can feel a bit strange. But for animals, and for many autistic people, silence isn’t empty. It’s a chance to breathe, to notice, to just be.
As we wrap up this chapter, let’s focus on empathy. Real understanding doesn’t always need words. Sometimes, it’s about tuning in, really paying attention, and being open to seeing the world through someone else’s eyes.
That’s the heart of communication. And honestly, it’s the foundation for every relationship that matters.
